title: LLM-driven agent behavior project
author: emergent-complexity
selftext:
I've been working on using an LLM as the "brain" of an agent in a 3D game setting. The goal is for the LLM to inform all aspects of agent behavior including both acting in the environment and dialogue, in real time. Not an easy task, as LLMs are a little clunky for this application. Inference is slow which affects agent reactiveness and converting real-time state and events into text is a clumsy process. Nevertheless, I have been grinding away at the problem for some time and have finished what I call version 2 of my LLM-Driven AI Agent. [Here ](https://youtu.be/dJqZ2uSII-c)is a demo video I put together. In the video, I play as the human character and use real-time speech-to-text to chat. The robot is entirely controlled by an LLM, for both behavior and speech.

Some highlights:

* Built in Unity
* Originally I was using a local LLM (Gemma3-4B) but progress was stalling, then I switched to a foundational model (Gemini3-flash) and the difference was stark. The agent started acting much more intelligently. Keep in mind this is a proof-of-concept so I'm not thinking about cost at the moment.
* The LLM works with a discrete action space (inspired somewhat by steering behaviors) to create a short-term plan. The plan can be interrupted at any time by environmental stimuli.
* Text-to-speech and speech-to-text both use their own neural networks, though they are not too processor-intensive.

In terms of gameplay I am keeping things simple for now as I try to work out the kinks of the system. I have plenty of ideas for improvement though, with the underlying architecture, gameplay and plot elements. That said it's coming along nicely. The video above was actually a first take - the agent was behaving well. I've had sessions as long as 20 minutes with interesting interactions and dialogue.

I would love to get some feedback on this project. Does this seem like interesting gameplay? Has anyone tried doing anything similar?

comments.author: Feisty-Dependent5336
comments.body: Hey I’ve been playing around this too. I think discrete action space is important. I tried more unrestricted and npcs were sending me on quests for items that don’t exist.

replies.author: emergent-complexity
replies.body: Agreed. When I first started the project I thought I would have the LLM output an open-ended short phrase and I'd use RAG to convert to an action. This turned out to be really hard so I switched to hard instructions for a set of specific actions. It is still an open question about how many actions I'll need. Actions are likely specific to the agent role. For example, "restrain" and "release" are used by this agent because it guards an area, but might not be used by all agents. I suppose I'll have to create action sets specific to each role, when I start making other roles that is!

replies.author: Feisty-Dependent5336
replies.body: Have you thought about utility functions for the agent?  E.g f(unauthorized visitors). I’m trying that as a grounding mechanism more like the sims and using llm for non mechanical decisions making

replies.author: emergent-complexity
replies.body:
I have not, but if I understand correctly, that would be used for selecting the most useful target to focus on? If that's the case, I would not need one because I'm keeping the scenario very simple for one. The player and one agent. It's already hard enough to get this simple scenario working in real-time so I going to try and get it right before adding another agent. 

Adding another agent reminds me of the [Three-body problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three-body_problem) in physics. It instantly adds a ton of complexity. I'm sure I will get there at some point, but not any time soon!

comments.author: Simple-Salt-1272
comments.body: Have you played AI Roguelite on steam? I would highly recommend it as it sounds very similar!

replies.author: emergent-complexity
replies.body:
I just checked it out. Not quite the same as that game seems to be more of a text adventure with images where the use can generate the scenario and everything is run by AI.

My project is made like a typical 3d game. That is, there is no generated content and the player enters the world as it was designed. But the NPC in the game (there is only one) is controlled by an LLM. The prompt contains game state and produces a plan of action in real-time. So there is no fixed behavior for the NPC. It is given a role and memories and it just acts in response to environmental stimuli.

replies.author: Simple-Salt-1272
replies.body: That is really interesting - I’m curious if you’re enforcing some type of output schema, and what kind of interval it makes these requests/decision at? The video was very interesting. I had some success trying to make a turn based game where you steer the llm every x turns, but this real time application is really impressive.

replies.author: emergent-complexity
replies.body:
Oh yes, the prompt is meticulously structured and so is the output. This took multiple iterations and it is still evolving. But the LLM seems pretty good at outputting the structured format, both with the local LLM and the cloud model. So that hasn't caused too much trouble. The hard part is turning real-time events into text. Like movement of the player for example. Not only is it clumsy to describe in text, but if I snapshot that information in a prompt and the prompt takes, say, 3 seconds to return, well lots can happen in 3 seconds of game time. I generally have to slow things down. The out-of-breath mechanic that you see in the video is one idea I had to slow things down.

As for prompt cadence, I basically have what would be called an event-driven behavior model. The LLM produces a short plan, the agent runs the plan and when that plan is finished it will create a new one. However, a plan can be interrupted at any time by an environmental event. For example, the agent seeing the player for the first time.

replies.author: Simple-Salt-1272
replies.body: Really awesome! I’ll be sure to keep an eye on your progress.

replies.author: emergent-complexity
replies.body: Thank you! The next step I think is to add more gameplay elements because it's kind of vanilla now. Like different ways to get past the agent beside the simple code word. I'll be sure to post on this board as I make progress.
